transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-13
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Carlos Vega (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood Solutions), Maya Chen (CTO, KiteLabs), Ravi Patel (Infra Lead), Sofia Martinez (Product), Jonas Weber (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
KiteLabs evaluating Redwood Dedicated reserved GPUs for production inference. Main concerns: tenant isolation, burst model for peak traffic (50-200% spikes), latency SLOs vs cost, encryption/KMS and SOC2 evidence, and fallback behavior to hosted models. Redwood to provide pricing/contract options, security pack, and benchmark plan.

Topics: scope of reserved capacity, isolation model (node vs tenant fencing), warm pools/pre-warm, burst handling and failover, telemetry/observability and cost breakdown, compliance/KMS and private deployment options, timeline for PoC and procurement requirements.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Carlos Vega: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Uh, this is the intake for KiteLabs — we wanted to go over dedicated capacity options, burst patterns, and the kind of isolation you're looking for. I'm Carlos, AE on the account.
[00:13] Maya Chen: Hi, Carlos. Thanks. I'm Maya, CTO. We'll try to keep it high level and then drill in. Our infra lead Ravi is here and Jonas is joining for security questions.
[00:21] Ravi Patel: Hey all. Quick context: KiteLabs runs a mixture of synchronous chat endpoints and batch embeddings for search. Peak RPS right now is around 450 requests/sec but we see spikes to 1200 during batch jobs and product launches. We need predictability.
[00:35] Priya Nambiar: Thanks Ravi. That's helpful. Are those spikes short lived (minutes) or multi-hour? Also what's your typical latency SLO for the chat endpoints?
[00:44] Ravi Patel: Spikes are usually 10-30 minutes during promo bursts, but sometimes an hour if ingestion spikes. Latency target is p95 < 650ms for our chat calls — and p99 ideally under 1.5s. We're sensitive to any tail latency.
[00:58] Sofia Martinez: From product side, uptime during these bursts is critical — we lose conversions otherwise. We also want a failover plan if reserved capacity is saturated.
[01:09] Priya Nambiar: High level on Redwood Dedicated: you get reserved GPU pools (we call them reserved nodes) that are isolated to your account. You can configure hot pre-warm pools that maintain a warm KV cache to reduce cold-start tail. For burst we offer two levers: reserved burst (burst units on top of reserved) and policy-based fallback to lower-cost/compatible hosts — or to a hosted model variant.
[01:33] Maya Chen: Can you elaborate on isolation? We're worried about noisy neighbors and data residency. Do dedicated nodes run in a shared cluster?
[01:41] Liam O'Connor: Good question. For Dedicated, the nodes are logically isolated and we support pinning entire GPU instances to a customer tenant in the cloud region. That means your workloads don't share GPU instances with other customers. We also offer VPC-private control plane for Private deployments if you need complete networking isolation on top of that.
[02:00] Jonas Weber: Does that include separate KMS or HSM integration? We have strict encryption key separation policies.
[02:06] Carlos Vega: Yes, we have KMS integrations and can map keys per-customer. For on-prem or private installs we support HSM integrations too. We'll share the security pack which contains the KMS options and redacted SOC2 docs.
[02:18] Ravi Patel: Good. On the burst side — if we exceed reserved capacity, what's the expected behavior? Do requests queue? Auto-scale? Fallback? How does billing look?
[02:27] Priya Nambiar: If you opt into our burst program, we can provision burst capacity that is chargeable above your commit at a known rate. Without it, the default is policy-based: requests that can't be served by reserved nodes can be routed to compatible model variants in our hosted fleet (if you enable that), or you can set strict deny/queue behavior. The routing respects latency SLOs — e.g., we won't route to a high-latency fallback unless you accept the tradeoff. Billing for burst is per-token/compute on top of reserved commit.
[02:52] Maya Chen: Hmm, we prefer not to route to the hosted fleet for PII workloads. We need guaranteed isolation for certain customers and for those calls we'd want hard reject or queued with SLA consequences. For non-PII traffic we could allow hosted fallback.
[03:08] Carlos Vega: Totally makes sense — you can define routes by tag/route: sensitive models go to Private or Dedicated-only endpoints; less-sensitive can have fallback to hosted or quantized variants. You can also set a per-route policy for queue length and reject thresholds.
[03:22] Sofia Martinez: About pre-warm — how many tokens or what memory needs to be warmed to get p95 numbers back down? We're seeing cold-starts of several seconds on large context.
[03:31] Priya Nambiar: Cold-starts are typically from KV cache not populated and kernel warmup. For chat workflows, maintaining a hot KV for your top flows reduces token latency dramatically. Pre-warm sizing depends on model size and sequence length; we'll recommend a warm pool size based on your traffic distribution. In practice, a small warm pool (2–4 GPUs prewarmed for high-volume routes) can hit p95 targets. We'll model this in the benchmark run.
[03:55] Ravi Patel: What's the warm-pool cost tradeoff? We have concerns about paying for idle GPUs.
[04:02] Liam O'Connor: Right — warm pools are reserved and count against your commit. We can structure the contract with a lower base commit plus a hot-pool add-on. We also support burst credits where you pre-pay for burst consumption at a discount relative to on-demand.
[04:16] Maya Chen: Procurement will want to see different commit levels and runway. Our legal team also wants to know preemption behavior and SLAs for evicting reserved nodes.
[04:25] Carlos Vega: We'll include a contract matrix showing minimums, burst rates, and SLAs. Reserved nodes are non-preemptible for Dedicated; preemption normally applies only in some private on-prem fragile configs.
[04:36] Jonas Weber: On audit logs and tracing — we need per-token tracing and audit logs for models that touch customer data. What's retained and how do we deliver logs?
[04:44] Priya Nambiar: Redwood Console provides token-level cost/latency breakdowns and per-request traces. Audit logs can be exported to your S3 or sent to a SIEM; retention is configurable. For PII flows we can enable redaction and only store metric-level aggregates if required.
[05:00] Ravi Patel: For the benchmark run — we will provide a representative synthetic trace and a sample of historical traffic. We want you to run both steady-state and chaotic spike tests.
[05:10] Priya Nambiar: Great. Our plan will include: first a baseline run on your current model (if you can share weights or a compatible binary) or on a close-matching open model, then prewarm sizing runs, and finally attack/spike tests with 5x traffic for short bursts. We'll surface p50/p95/p99 and token cost.
[05:29] Maya Chen: A couple of more technical questions: do you support mixed precision/quantized runtimes, and is there any degradation on hallucination quality? We have QA gating on model quality.
[05:40] Liam O'Connor: We support multiple quant profiles (8-bit, 4-bit where applicable) and runtime kernels tuned for those profiles. Quality regressions depend on model architecture and prompt set. It's why Redwood Optimize gives recommendations and you can A/B test model variants with traffic splitting. We also hook evals to capture QA regressions.
[05:58] Sofia Martinez: Are rollouts and canary supported so we can test new model versions during peak windows?
[06:04] Priya Nambiar: Yes — rollouts, canary, and automatic fallback policies are all supported. You can do time-based canaries or traffic-percent rollouts; the console shows latency and quality metrics per variant.
[06:13] Ravi Patel: Regarding network topology — we run in AWS in us-west-2. We need low intra-VPC latency; will Dedicated nodes be in our account VPC or in Redwood-managed VPC with peering?
[06:24] Carlos Vega: For Dedicated we have two options: managed VPC peering (fast and easier) or Private deployment where the control plane is customer-managed and nodes run in your VPC/account. For strict network isolation and compliance, Private is preferred; otherwise peered Dedicated nodes hit low latencies.
[06:40] Jonas Weber: One last compliance note — we have a list of control requirements around key rotation, key custody, and encryption in transit. We'll share the list.
[06:47] Carlos Vega: Noted — Jonas, please send that. We'll have our security team respond.
[06:51] Maya Chen: On timeline: procurement needs to see numbers by next week ideally. We're aiming to close a committed capacity deal before the end of the quarter (end of March). Is that feasible?
[06:59] Carlos Vega: If we get the traffic profile and confirmation on the commit level this week, we can produce a tailored pricing matrix and SLA and hit procurement review next week. Implementation-wise, Dedicated spin-up is usually 2–3 weeks after contract signature, shorter for peered Dedicated.
[07:12] Ravi Patel: For PoC benchmarks, will you need any secrets or access into our environment? We prefer not to hand over sensitive keys.
[07:19] Priya Nambiar: We can run benchmarks using synthetic traffic and redacted payloads. If you want an in-VPC latency test we can set up a short-lived bastion or use a signed runner that you host. We don't require long-lasting credentials.
[07:31] Sofia Martinez: Cost question for long-running batch embeddings — we run big weekly batches that spike GPU usage. Can we do scheduled batch windows to avoid paying higher burst rates?
[07:41] Liam O'Connor: Yes. You can reserve capacity sized for peak batch throughput or schedule batch jobs into cheaper off-peak windows. Also, Dedicated supports job-scheduling policies where you can pre-allocate for nightly windows.
[07:53] Maya Chen: Any hard limits on model sizes for Dedicated? We have a few models ~70B params.
[07:59] Priya Nambiar: We support up to the largest modern open families; model sharding across multiple GPUs works and we have tuned kernels for large model inference. We'll check specifics for your 70B models in the benchmark planning.
[08:10] Ravi Patel: What about autoscaling latency? If we get a sudden 5x increase, how fast do you scale and at what granularity?
[08:18] Priya Nambiar: Autoscaling for Dedicated can add reserved burst capacity in minutes depending on available hot capacity; for instant spikes we rely on warm pools and pre-provisioned burst units. We also support multi-region failover for very large spikes. Realistically, scaling a new GPU into production takes some minutes to tens of minutes depending on provisioning.
[08:36] Maya Chen: Okay. For procurement we'll need an example SLO clause and credits for SLA misses.
[08:42] Carlos Vega: We'll attach an SLA appendix with credits tiers.
[08:46] Jonas Weber: Please make sure the security pack includes details on key separation, customer KMS mappings, audit log formats, and retention.
[08:54] Carlos Vega: Will do.
[08:57] Sofia Martinez: Can we run a small paid pilot to validate prewarm and p95 numbers before committing to a big reserved contract?
[09:05] Carlos Vega: Absolutely — our standard approach is a time-boxed pilot with a small reserved footprint and defined testcases. We can convert pilot usage to commit within the contract.
[09:14] Maya Chen: Great. Let's talk next steps.

Action recap at ~09:23
[09:23] Carlos Vega: Recap — Redwood to send: 1) Pricing matrix with commit tiers and burst pricing; 2) Security pack (SOC2 summary, KMS options); 3) Benchmark plan and proposed dates; 4) Contract template and SLA appendix. KiteLabs to send: traffic profile, SLO targets, list of compliance controls, and decision-makers for procurement.
[09:42] Maya Chen: Sounds good. We'll try to get traffic artifacts and procurement contacts today.
[09:48] Ravi Patel: I'll prepare traffic traces and a sample of payloads (redacted).
[09:52] Jonas Weber: I'll collect the compliance list and questions and send them over.
[09:56] Carlos Vega: We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the benchmark run. Priya will run the technical planning session with Ravi and team.
[10:03] Priya Nambiar: I'll send an agenda for the benchmark run, including test cases (steady, 2x, 5x spike, long-tail stress), metrics we'll capture, and what artifacts we need from KiteLabs.
[10:13] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. That's all from KiteLabs.
[10:16] Carlos Vega: Thanks — we'll get these docs over and schedule times. Appreciate it.

Closing notes (auto-gen): Meeting ran ~62 minutes. Most of time was product/architecture Q&A and scope alignment. Clear next steps and POC/benchmark plan defined.
